webTitle: Morning Mail: One Nation sleepovers at Rinehart’s revealed, Japan trips getting more expensive, and more AI alarm

fields.headline: Morning Mail: One Nation sleepovers at Rinehart’s revealed, Japan trips getting more expensive, and more AI alarm
fields.trailText: New podcast looks at who One Nation really stands for; scrutiny over Australia’s military exports; AI bosses back calls to slow development
fields.bodyText: Good morning. Today we launch The Populist: a podcast about how One Nation is gaining ground in Australia. The four-part series follows senior correspondent Sarah Martin as she uncovers the inner workings of Pauline Hanson’s One Nation – a party that has imported the modus operandi of the global populist right, including Trump-style attacks on the media. The Populist asks who One Nation really stands for and what influence its billionaire benefactor Gina Rinehart has over the party. Elsewhere there’s speculation over the intended target of a Russian drone strike near the Ukraine-Poland border. And tech titans, including Elon Musk, say they’ll back calls to pump the brakes on AI development. Australia ‘Red lines’ legislation | David Pocock is among crossbench MPs who will pressure Labor to ban Australian goods from being used by the Israeli military. Sleepover at Rinehart’s | One Nation’s Pauline Hanson and Barnaby Joyce stayed overnight at Gina Rinehart’s Brisbane mansion after fundraising events, with Joyce conducting a live television interview about politics from the $20m home. He did not declare the hospitality to parliament because the billionaire is a “long-term friend”. End of the road? | The Japanese yen has now reached its highest level against the US and Australian dollars in six months. Is the era of budget-friendly trips coming to an end for Australian travellers? ‘They can get to incredible numbers’ | Rabbits are the biggest threat to Australia’s native species. And due to good rainfall and growing resistance to viruses, rabbit populations are booming. Sea lion death | South Australia has recorded the first death of an endangered Australian sea lion from H5 bird flu, amid fears for the protected species of which less than 12,000 remain nationwide. World Russia-Ukraine war | A train carrying former UK PM Boris Johnson and ex-CIA chief David Petraeus may have been the intended target of a drone strike near the Poland-Ukraine border, officials say. AI alarm | Sam Altman and Elon Musk have backed a call from the head of Anthropic to “slow the pace” of AI development in a rare show of unity from rival developers. “Too little, too late”: critics remain suspicious of AI leaders’ call for a slowdown. Middle East crisis | A pregnant woman was among more than 10 killed in Israeli strikes on Gaza; Iran-allied Houthis have said they used drones and missiles to attack a military base in Saudi Arabia. Buying votes? | Donald Trump has doubled down on his controversial pledge to give US adults a “dividend” if his Republican ⁠party keeps control of Congress after November’s midterm elections. Sweden votes | Results are too close to call in Sweden’s high-stakes election, with projections narrowing after exit polls initially showed the centre-left bloc was set to take power over the incumbent centre-right coalition. Follow updates on our live blog. Full Story The Populist: Aeroplanes and bulldozers | Episode 1 “If you’re trying to say I’m being funded by Gina Rinehart, the answer is no.” That’s what One Nation leader Pauline Hanson told the Guardian’s senior correspondent Sarah Martin in February. We now know that’s not true. Over months, Martin pieced together flight tracking data and expense records to uncover the true extent of financial support flowing from Australia’s richest person to the country’s fastest growing political force. Episode one of the Populist podcast, launched today, tells the inside story, from the Farrer byelection to the National Press Club – including exclusive new reporting. In-depth As peer-on-peer violence continues to rise, many girls, who make up the majority of school-age sexual assault victims, have no choice but to return to school. And in many cases, they must continue to share a campus with their assailant. When schools must balance a duty of care to both victims and perpetrators, where does this leave girls who have to pursue their education in the shadow of sexual assault? Not the news With a busy touring schedule of Brisbane, Melbourne and Sydney ahead, the Fijian Flying Circus is a lo-fi, high energy mix that teaches its performers a valuable grab-bag of theatre and life skills even as they charm the crowds. The most important thing for the performers, however, is what is happening back at home. Once salaries are paid, every extra dollar goes into funding the next generation of Fijian circus performers. Sport Tennis | Alexander Zverev is facing Ben Shelton in this year’s US Open men’s singles final; Elena Rybakina rode the “ups and downs” to transform her status among tennis elite, Tumaini Carayol writes. AFL | The Lions have been rewarded for embracing risk as “good Brisbane” keeps the AFL flag dream alive, Jonathan Horn writes. Football | Manchester City recovered from Phil Foden red card as Erling Haaland won the derby at United; Lewis Dunk’s showstopper helped five-star Brighton to rout 10-man Coventry in the Premier League. Motorsport | Kimi Antonelli held off Max Verstappen during his Madring debut to win the F1 Spanish Grand Prix. Cycling | Enric Mas reigns supreme at last in the Vuelta a España to delight Spanish fans. Rugby union | Greatest Rivalry swagger showed South Africa will take some beating at the World Cup, Gerard Meagher writes. Media roundup Australia is spending $27bn to build three warships to replace the aging Anzac-class ships. Will the project be worth it?, asks ABC News. Australians paid more than five times the benchmark price for a visit to a specialist doctor on more than a million occasions last year, the SMH reports. Documents have revealed how Labor supercharged the use of contingency funding for major infrastructure projects in Victoria, the Age reports. What’s happening today ACT | Federal parliament is sitting in Canberra. NSW | The trial of former broadcaster Alan Jones continues in Sydney. Sign up Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email If you would like to receive this Morning Mail update to your email inbox every weekday, sign up here, or finish your day with our Politics, really newsletter, where our political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for you.. You can follow the latest in US politics by signing up for This Week in Trumpland. Brain teaser And finally, here are the Guardian’s crosswords to keep you entertained throughout the day. Until tomorrow. Quick crossword Cryptic crossword

webTitle: The American emperor’s new clothes? | Brief letters

fields.headline: The American emperor’s new clothes?
fields.trailText: Brief letters: Trump’s toga | Reform UK donations | Ben Delo | Word watch | Andy Burnham | The name game
fields.bodyText: Octavian (later Emperor Augustus), following his victorious battles of Illyricum and Actium, announced he would give 400 sesterces to adult male citizens. Will we see the US president wearing an emperor’s purple and gold toga soon (Trump promise of $5,000 for US citizens after midterms decried as ‘bribery’, 10 September)? David Shannon Ashton under Hill, Worcestershire • Can we assume that the donations to Reform UK from the billionaires Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo (Report, 12 September) will be followed by some sort of cash offer for every adult in the UK should Mr Farage win the next election? Phil Thomas Frodsham, Cheshire • The crypto-billionaire Ben Delo told the Telegraph he wanted “a level playing field”. Presumably the cheques for the Greens and Lib Dems are lost in the post. Tim Mansfield Galgate, Lancaster • After “wild swimming” and “vertical drinking”, Joe Hyde asks: “Whatever next?” (Letters, 9 September). We have known the answer for ages: “lived experience”. Charles Foster Chalfont St Peter, Buckinghamshire • George Monbiot asks why Andy Burnham is taking a huge risk with fossil fuels (Opinion, 10 September). Maybe it is just another example of nominative determinism (Letters, 10 September). Andy Cook Honley, West Yorkshire • I am delighted to see that the nominative determinism discussion is getting out of hand. Frank Lawless Leeds • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

webTitle: Obama reportedly urges Democrats to prioritize safety plan for AI

fields.headline: Obama reportedly urges Democrats to prioritize safety plan for AI
fields.trailText: Ex-president urged party at closed-door fundraiser to create sweeping framework, from safety ‘slow-down’ to job losses
fields.bodyText: Barack Obama urged Democrats to prioritize a “public conversation” about AI management and safety in a closed-door Manhattan fundraiser last week. The comments by the former US president reportedly urged the party to create a sweeping framework for everything from a safety “slow-down” to domestic job losses and children’s wellbeing. Obama’s comments follow a summer in which a band of rogue OpenAI chatbots hacked the company Hugging Face, towns across the country opposed datacenters and an AI researcher resigned in a viral social media post warning: “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.” AI leaders have recently expressed agreement that the race for technological superiority should slow, but have also sought to appease investors, whose stake in the technology is predicted to exceed $1tn in 2026 alone. “Once you are speaker,” Obama said to US House minority leader Hakeem Jeffries, a New York-Democrat, at the fundraiser Thursday. “I would strongly urge that the Democrats put together a framework for a very public conversation,” according to a transcript first reported by the New York Times. “This is something that is moving very fast in private hands, and if we don’t get on top of it, I think can be dangerous,” Obama said. “If we do get on top of it, I do think it’s beneficial. I genuinely think it’s going to accelerate, for example, drug development in ways that can help us cure diseases. I do think that this can help us figure out pathways for a clean energy future.” Obama later added: “I would talk about this, and I would say, ‘Here’s our plan for safety. Here’s our plan for making sure our kids are not corrupted by this,’” he said according to the Times. Obama made the remarks as the US closes in on the midterm elections and Congress has taken little action on AI. While prominent Democratic lawmakers, and some Republicans, have called to regulate the technology, Trump has attempted to aid the AI industry by introducing legislation that would ban state regulations (the bill did not move forward). Democrats face an open presidential field in 2028. One major flashpoint for the midterm elections is datacenters that power AI companies. Both parties have since begun running ads that oppose them, as one of the few issues, “Maga Republicans and liberal Democrats” agree on, according to an NPR analysis. On Sunday, while on a trip to his Irish golf course, Trump told reporters that a lot of “very negative forces” are ⁠bringing up concerns ⁠about AI that “won’t happen”, and that his main concern was that the US remain the industry leader, according to Reuters. “We’re leading China in AI. ‌We’re the ‌most sophisticated country in the world, ‌and frankly I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI wins,” Trump told reporters when asked if ‌the AI industry should slow down or be more regulated. In the past, Trump has said on social media that anyone who opposes AI datacenters is likely “backwards and poor”. “The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor. If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign,” he said on TruthSocial two weeks ago.

webTitle: ‘It’s just straight bigotry’: wave of Islamophobic rhetoric looms over US midterm elections

fields.headline: ‘It’s just straight bigotry’: wave of Islamophobic rhetoric looms over US midterm elections
fields.trailText: As Muslims win historic victories, experts describe rise in anti-Islamic sentiment that rivals post-9/11 climate
fields.bodyText: Within hours of Abdul El-Sayed’s victory in Michigan’s Democratic US Senate primary, Republican senator Tommy Tuberville of Alabama declared that the party had “just voted to send a TERRORIST” to Washington. El-Sayed – or “Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed”, as Tuberville called him on X – was a “RADICAL ISLAMIST” who would “do everything he can to destroy America”, he claimed. It was the opening shot in what researchers who track anti-Muslim sentiment describe as the most concentrated wave of Islamophobic rhetoric in US electoral politics since the 9/11 attacks, arriving at the exact moment Muslim candidates are winning office in unprecedented numbers. “It’s probably the worst of what we’ve seen,” said Saher Selod, director of research at the non-partisan Institute for Social Policy and Understanding (ISPU), which has tracked anti-Muslim sentiment nationally for a decade. “We’re certainly seeing in 2025 and 2026, ahead of these midterms, really very Islamophobic ads – more so than what we saw after 9/11.” ISPU’s 2025 Islamophobia Index, a 100-point scale built using common anti-Muslim stereotypes, rose from 25 in 2022 to 33 among the general public in 2025, with the sharpest increases among white and Hispanic Americans. The Pew Research Center found in a survey this spring that 51% of US adults now say Islam is more likely than other religions to encourage violence, up from just 25% six months after the 2001 attacks. The partisan gap on that question has widened sharply. Back in 2002, 32% of likely Republican voters and 23% of Democrats said Islam was more likely than other religions to encourage violence, according to the Pew survey. Today, 76% of Republicans say the same, and 29% of Democrats. Anti-Muslim hate crimes reported to the FBI, which spiked to 481 in 2001 from 28 the year before, have never returned to pre-2001 levels, according to Pew’s research. The ISPU separately found that 63% of Muslims reported experiencing religious discrimination in the past year, the highest share of any faith group it measures. Set against that backdrop is a wave of Muslim electoral success. There are four Muslim members of US Congress, with a fifth likely on the way, compared with zero in 2001. Ghazala Hashmi became Virginia’s first Muslim woman elected to statewide office this year, as lieutenant governor. Zohran Mamdani was inaugurated as New York’s first Muslim mayor in January 2025, and El-Sayed’s primary win put him on track to potentially become the first Muslim ever elected to the US Senate. The reaction to El-Sayed’s victory showed how quickly the rhetoric escalates. The Center for the Study of Organized Hate found Islamophobic posts naming El-Sayed rose by nearly 1,900% in the week after his win, from an average of 155 to more than 3,000 a day. The attacks are also coming from the very top of the Republican party. Donald Trump infamously called in 2015 for a “total and complete shutdown” on Muslims entering the US when he was running for president, and attempted to enact one via executive order in early 2017. After years of legal wrangling, the supreme court did allow Trump to implement a limited version of his travel restrictions for majority Muslim countries. This year, Trump called El-Sayed a “jihadist” from the Oval Office, and separately claimed – without naming anyone – that “jihadists” were being elected to office “all over the place”. Vice-president JD Vance, meanwhile, called El-Sayed “very, very evil” at a Michigan rally and, separately, invoked his own late grandfather to attack comments El-Sayed made in 2022 defending a legal challenge to an Oklahoma anti-Sharia ballot measure. The attacks go beyond one candidate, however. Senator Ted Cruz told Fox News that El-Sayed and Mamdani were “Islamists” who “want Sharia law” and “hate Jews, they hate Christians, they hate capitalism, they hate America”. Representative Nancy Mace posted that “every single Muslim holding public office in America is a trojan horse, and a threat to both national security and our republic”, and followed up by writing that Islam “must be removed from civil society in the US”. In March, Representative Randy Fine of Florida wrote on X, “We need more Islamophobia, not less. Fear of Islam is rational,” while Representative Andy Ogles of Tennessee posted that “Muslims don’t belong in American society”. Republican leadership has been mostly silent. For Mobashra Tazamal, associate director of Georgetown University’s Bridge Initiative, which studies Islamophobia globally, the shift is shockingly noticeable. “It is almost as if the veil has been lifted,” she said. “It is so bigoted, and it’s so crude, and there is no red line. It’s just straight bigotry.” *** The rhetoric has also extended beyond individual candidates into policy fights. In Texas, Governor Greg Abbott has spent much of the summer campaigning against what he calls the imposition of Islamic law, ordering a review of state grants to two major airports and referring both to federal regulators over privately funded wudu stations, ritual washing facilities Muslims use before prayer, which he called illegal religious favoritism. Abbott has separately fought a proposed mosque-anchored housing development outside Dallas. Nationally, the Center for the Study of Organized Hate documented a coordinated campaign among 89 elected officials over 13 months, including 1,111 social media posts and eight bills, tied to a “Sharia Free America Caucus” that has grown to 65 members. The anti-Sharia campaigns are not new: close to two dozen states passed largely symbolic anti-Sharia laws in the early 2010s. “This isn’t an issue. It’s not something that’s real,” said Tazamal. “It’s constructed, and then these politicians claim to be tackling this constructed problem that they create.” The picture is complicated, though. Researchers caution against treating every attack on El-Sayed or Mamdani as bigotry. El-Sayed drew criticism – including from Vance – after he responded to a March attack on a suburban Detroit synagogue by saying “hurt people hurt people”, noting that relatives of the attacker in Lebanon had recently been killed in an Israeli airstrike. El-Sayed eventually apologized, and said the remarks may have been misconstrued. He has also faced scrutiny over his public association with the hyper-popular leftwing streamer Hasan Piker, who mainstream Democrats and Republicans have attacked for past comments minimizing the 11 September attacks. Mamdani has faced sustained criticism, including from rivals in his own mayoral race, over his refusal to unequivocally condemn the phrase “globalize the intifada”, a phrase Jewish groups say amounts to a call for violence against Jews, but one that he has never personally used. Mamdani subsequently said he would discourage the term after a rabbi told him it evokes memories of bus bombings and restaurant attacks for many Jewish New Yorkers. The controversy among Jewish organizations, rival campaigns and national Democrats, was not, in the end, disqualifying in the eyes of voters who ultimately decided the race. The devastation in Gaza, mass settler violence in the West Bank and the suppression of pro-Palestine speech in the US has brought an additional dimension to this discourse. US opinion on Israel has soured immensely in recent years, especially among Democrats, and criticism of Israeli policy by the likes of El-Sayed and Mamdani is cited by those describing Muslim politicians “jihadists”. Mahmoud Khalil, Rümeysa Öztürk and other Muslim residents in the US were among the first swept up for pro-Palestinian campus advocacy, even though most of the students protesting were not Muslim. That pattern, criticism aimed at religious identity rather than positions or votes, is consistent with what researchers have documented since well before this election cycle. And the point, Selod and Tazamal say, is whether that criticism is being used as cover for a broader claim – that Muslim identity itself, not any specific position on issue or another, is disqualifying from US public life. “With Abdul El-Sayed, we’re seeing these kinds of intense Islamophobic attacks against him, as opposed to attacking his platform or critiquing his policies,” Selod said. “It’s a playbook. They’re going to attack him for his religious identity to see if this will help pull voters away from him.” That playbook resurfaced this week in New York, where Mamdani attended the ceremony marking Friday’s 25th anniversary of 9/11 at Ground Zero, as his predecessors have every year. A petition with more than 100,000 signatures, riddled with attacks, unashamedly asked him not to. Rudy Giuliani, mayor of New York City at the time of the attacks, who is now closely aligned to Trump, claimed from thin air that Mamdani “doesn’t agree that September 11 was an Islamic terrorist attack”, and that his attendance “offends” him, adding even more venom against Muslims generally: “They have every desire to take us over … they want to dominate us. Mamdani is a clear supporter of that.” Giuliani offered no evidence for either claim. Cheri Sparacio, one of the petition’s organizers, whose husband died in the attacks, has said her objection is “not about the mayor’s background or faith, but his public actions”. Mamdani attended anyway, and on Friday morning, Mamdani and Giuliani shook hands at the ceremony. *** Yet the current moment cannot be separated from the infrastructure built after 9/11, Selod said. “All of the surveillance programs that were put into place, your no-fly list, ICE – these are a product of 9/11,” she said. “We didn’t have Immigration and Customs Enforcement. We didn’t have the TSA, the Transportation Security Administration. These were all put into place to protect the nation against threats of terrorism.” That architecture has since been extended well past its original target, Selod argued, pointing to the Boston Regional Intelligence Center, a post-9/11 “fusion center” built to detect terrorist plots. Local reporting and ACLU of Massachusetts records show the center has also been used to monitor Black Lives Matter demonstrators. “It’s expanding beyond a Muslim population to target others,” she said. “Muslims are one to two percent of the US population. My hope is when people start to see how it’s expanding beyond that population, maybe they’ll start really critiquing these programs.” ISPU polling suggests the sentiment tracks politics rather than faith. Americans who identify as somewhat or very conservative are 13 percentage points more likely than others to endorse anti-Muslim stereotypes, the ISPU found, while religiosity shows no correlation. Tazamal ties the current spike partly to political calculation. “Polling for Trump is low, and the GOP is the sitting party, and they haven’t delivered on their promises,” she said. “So instead of focusing on institutional failures and policies they haven’t been able to put into place, they’re stirring up hate and bigotry towards a certain group, which is a routine tactic that they do.” Caleb Elfenbein, a Grinnell College professor who has mapped Islamophobic rhetoric for years, sees a small, organized network reactivating on a predictable schedule. “It really looks, and feels, like a very cynical effort to take advantage of a general sense of fear that can be activated at any given time,” he said. Whether it works for a GOP that polling indicates is likely to face heavy losses in November’s midterm elections is the open question hanging over this campaign. Republicans are simultaneously contending with an unpopular war with Iran and rising costs that have squeezed their approval ratings. Whatever happens, amid growing political mobilization among Muslim Americans and other groups, Tazamal does not expect the party to abandon this effort, or the Islamophobic rhetoric at the center of it. “I don’t think the GOP is going to do away with it,” she said. • This article was amended on 15 September 2026 to clarify the date of polling carried out by the Pew Research Center.

webTitle: Trump reiterates $5,000 ‘dividend’ pledge if Republicans win midterms

fields.headline: Trump reiterates $5,000 ‘dividend’ pledge if Republicans win midterms
fields.trailText: Plan to give US adults $5,000 has been greeted with incredulity across the political spectrum as well as outrage
fields.bodyText: Donald Trump has doubled down on his controversial pledge to give US adults a $5,000 “dividend” if his Republican ⁠party keeps control of Congress after November’s midterm elections. The plan has been greeted with expressions of incredulity across the US political spectrum as well as outraged accusations of seeking to bribe voters. The proposal – which would cost more than a trillion dollars – also comes amid huge concern over the US national debt, which topped $40tn for the first time in August. “I don’t ‌know but ‌it’s easy if the ‌Republicans win. $5,000 to all adults in the country and we can easily handle that because we’re taking in ‌so much money,” Trump told reporters in Ireland, where he is on a visit to his golf course in Doonbeg. Trump had been asked if Congress would need to approve the $5,000 pledge. He said: “The Democrats can’t make that pledge ⁠because it would all go to hell right away, we’d go into a depression … ‌I made that pledge, I always keep my pledge.” The US has roughly 240 million adult citizens, suggesting a cost of $1.2tn. The federal government spent about $7tn in fiscal year 2025, with about $2tn taken on as debt. When the plan was first touted by Trump last week at a rally in Texas, Marc Goldwein of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget wrote on X: “The result would be a huge spike in the deficit, and almost certainly in the inflation rate.” Democratic political leaders also reacted with a mix of outrage, disbelief and condemnation to the remarkable suggestion, which comes at a time when Trump is struggling with low poll numbers and a disastrous conflict in Iran, which is having an impact on the health of the US economy. “After making you sicker and poorer with his war, Donald Trump now wants to buy your vote with $5,000 in taxpayer-funded blood money,” said California governor Gavin Newsom. “The most corrupt man ever to occupy the Oval Office.” Some Republicans have backed the idea. “I will get a bill ready so that we can get the Trump Dividend passed immediately after the November 3rd election,” said US senator Bernie Moreno, an Ohio Republican, in a social media post on X. Any such payment would have ‌to be approved by Congress. On Sunday Mike Johnson, the House speaker and a Louisiana Republican, told CNN: “Of course, the devil’s in the ‌details. We have to figure all that out.” But Democratic politicians on Sunday morning talkshows in the US dismissed the idea. Hakeem Jeffries, the House minority leader, told ABC’s This Week that the plan was not a “serious proposal”. Reuters and the Associated Press contributed reporting

webTitle: ‘Trump accounts’ promise to mint child millionaires. Experts have their doubts

fields.headline: ‘Trump accounts’ promise to mint child millionaires. Experts have their doubts
fields.trailText: President has hyped growth of federal investment accounts to help US children – for his own political gain
fields.bodyText: Since returning to the White House, Donald Trump has scrapped rules that made childcare more affordable and pushed to cut funding for the nation’s public schools. But with midterm elections fast approaching and his approval ratings very low, the US president has repeatedly trumpeted a two-month-old program designed to help the nation’s children. That program, unhumbly named “Trump accounts”, calls for the federal government to give a one-time $1,000 seed deposit to every newborn whose family applies. In campaign speeches this summer, Trump has sought to milk these accounts for maximum political advantage, making big promises about how much these accounts will help the nation’s children. In a speech in Las Vegas last month, Trump hailed the program, saying: “It’s really giving [children] a head start on the American dream… They start off with $1,000 … and they can end up with $100,000, $200,000, $300,000” and if the stock market booms, “you’d end up with $1m”. With these accounts, Trump seems to want to come across as a Santa Claus stuffing $1,000 into every newborn’s stocking (although that money comes from the federal government). He and other Republicans boast that these accounts will significantly lift up all children, including children from low-income families, and also narrow the wealth gap between rich and poor. When Trump kicked off these accounts in early July, the treasury department said: “Trump Accounts level the playing field by allowing every parent to invest in their children’s future, not just wealthy families with trust funds.” A big problem, however, is that many economists say Trump’s claims about these accounts are vastly exaggerated or false. As Trump seeks to excite voters about these accounts, he has hyped how much they will grow, especially with regard to non-affluent families who don’t have the wherewithal to deposit money into these tax-deferred accounts to help their children. In his speeches, Trump sometimes gives the inaccurate impression that a newborn’s account with a $1,000 seed deposit will mushroom to $200,000 or $300,000 by the time the child turns 18, even when that child’s family doesn’t have money to make subsequent deposits. What’s more, “Trump accounts” are likely to increase, not decrease, the wealth gap between rich and poor. These accounts have definite tax advantages for wealthier families, who, unlike most low-income or working-class families, are able to make the maximum $5,000 deposit allowed each year into these tax-deferred accounts. It’s the families rich enough to contribute $5,000 a year who could see their children’s accounts grow to $200,000 or $300,000, far outstripping the accounts of children from poorer families. “This policy is not about giving poor kids a leg up. It’s more likely to widen the gap between rich and poor,” said Justin Wolfers, an economics professor at the University of Michigan, in a video. Kush Desai, a White House spokesperson, said in an email: “Trump Accounts are already shaping up to make a generational difference for working-class children who have not historically benefitted from traditional tax advantaged accounts.” He noted that the billionaires Michael Dell and Ray Dalio, as well as multinational corporations, have “pledged to donate billions of dollars of their wealth to the Trump Accounts of working-class children”. Desai rejected any assertions that the program would increase inequality, saying: “High income parents have always had an array of tools to grow wealth for their kids, but Trump Accounts are giving middle class parents the same opportunity – with billionaires chipping in to help. Only a moron would argue billionaires giving money away to working-class kids will worsen inequality.” The Trump administration has hyped the accounts with extremely optimistic claims. A White House website forecasts that many children with “Trump accounts” will have $271,000 in their account by age 18 and $13m by age 55. That sounds fabulous, but according to Wolfers, those big numbers are based on an impressive 10% annual rate of return for decades – a rate of return that is extraordinarily hard to achieve year after year. Moreover, those higher numbers are for children whose parents put in $5,000 annually until age 18, and then $7,000 a year when their children are in their 20s. Wolfers derided these White House estimates, saying in his video: “They’re ridiculous, they’re dishonest and they’re misleading.” Administration officials defended their estimates of how much the accounts would grow, saying those estimates are “not dissimilar to similar projections issued by retirement account providers”. In his speeches, Trump omits something important: he fails to note that for families unable to contribute beyond the initial $1,000 seed deposit, that amount would, according to White House estimates, grow to $6,000 by age 18. (That too is also based an optimistic 10% annual return.) No one should pooh-pooh a government-given deposit of $1,000 or a possible $6,000 at age 18. But Darrick Hamilton, a New School economics professor and one of the inventors of the baby bonds idea, said those amounts are too small to change the life of a child in need – too small to make college affordable or to buy a house. “It’s really an income transfer, not a wealth-building tool,” Hamilton said. He said it is the wealthiest 20%, especially the top 10%, who save money, while “people in the bottom 80% are usually dis-savers, they’re usually borrowers.” In other words, he said, the richest 20% will benefit from the tax breaks by depositing $5,000 a year into Trump accounts for their children. “The main mechanism for these accounts is active savings by parents, and that’s by nature regressive,” Hamilton said. “These accounts will actually increase wealth inequality because they favor people wealthy enough to have money to put into savings.” As part of the program, employers can contribute $2,500 a year to the account of an employee’s child. That $2,500 becomes a nice tax break for well-paid employees – the $2,500 contribution won’t be counted as taxable income. As a result, high-income workers in higher tax brackets will receive bigger tax breaks than lower-paid workers. The $1,000 seed deposits for newborns – the main part of the program helping the non-affluent – are to expire when Trump’s second term ends. But the parts of the program that help the wealthy most – the tax deferrals and tax breaks – are to continue indefinitely. Many Republicans and business executives have hailed “Trump accounts” as a way to make American children participants in the capitalist system. Senator Ted Cruz said: “Trump accounts are, in many ways, Donald Trump’s New Deal – but instead of having government taking care of everyone, Trump accounts are about making every child and every American a capitalist.” Hamilton sees things differently. Noting that Trump accounts are invested in the stock market, he said: “This is part of their larger plan to privatize our social safety net. This is in line with Republican plans to dismantle social security.” Senator Cory Booker and Representative Ayanna Pressley introduced a never-enacted baby bonds bill in 2019 under which children would receive $1,000 in their birth year and up to $2,000 more every year to age 18. Under their proposal, based on ideas from Hamilton and the Duke professor William Darity, lower-income families would receive larger government contributions than affluent ones. Children from families at the poverty level would see their accounts rise to an estimated $46,000 by age 18, about three times as much as children from families making twice the poverty line and more than 20 times as much as children from wealthy families. Hamilton said giving larger deposits to children from poorer families would give those kids more of a leg up. But that’s not the program that Trump and the Republican-controlled Congress approved.
